kapak.alt: How does the brain rebuild balance?

youtube.baslik: How Vestibular Compensation Works | Lesson 258 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
After a unilateral vestibular loss, the brain gradually rebuilds balance. In this lesson we cover static and dynamic compensation, rebalancing in the vestibular nuclei, the role of the cerebellum, the routes of adaptation, substitution and habituation, the time course, and factors that delay the process, such as vestibular suppressant drugs.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Jacobson and Shepard, Balance Function Assessment and Management; Herdman and Clendaniel, Vestibular Rehabilitation; Lacour and Bernard-Demanze, Interaction between vestibular compensation mechanisms and vestibular rehabilitation therapy: 10 recommendations for optimal functional recovery, Frontiers in Neurology (2015); Lacour, Helmchen and Vidal, Vestibular compensation: the neuro-otologist's best friend, Journal of Neurology (2016); Hall et al., Vestibular rehabilitation for peripheral vestibular hypofunction: an updated clinical practice guideline, Journal of Neurologic Physical Therapy (2022).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: How does the brain rebuild balance?
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how the brain rebuilds balance after a unilateral vestibular loss, that is, vestibular compensation.
We will cover static and dynamic compensation, the routes of central plasticity and the factors that delay the process.

sahneler.baslik: When the two sides are not *in balance*
cumleler: With the head still, the vestibular nerves on both sides fire continuously, with equal resting activity.
The vestibular nuclei in the brainstem constantly compare this activity from the two sides.
When a sudden loss occurs on one side, for example in vestibular neuritis, the activity from that side drops abruptly.
The nuclei interpret this imbalance as the head turning continuously toward the healthy side.
The result is intense vertigo, spontaneous nystagmus beating toward the healthy side and a tendency to fall toward the affected side.
Activity in the nuclei on the affected side drops not only because of the nerve loss, but also because of inhibition from the other side.
Compensation is the process by which the brain reduces this imbalance over time.
Symptoms after the loss fall into two groups; static symptoms are present even with the head still.
Spontaneous nystagmus, constant vertigo and a slight tilt of the head and body are static symptoms.
The reduction of static symptoms is called static compensation.
Dynamic symptoms appear when the head moves; with fast head movement toward the affected side, the image slips and balance is upset.
The reduction of these symptoms is called dynamic compensation.
The two processes progress at different speeds and rely on different mechanisms.
After a sudden loss on the right, the spontaneous nystagmus beats to the left, toward the healthy side, as in this example.
In the first days, the nystagmus is marked and may not be fully suppressed even by visual fixation.
As static compensation progresses, the nystagmus decreases quickly; first it becomes visible only when fixation is removed.
So with Frenzel or video goggles, a mild nystagmus may still be seen after compensation.
Stimuli such as head shaking can bring back, for a while, an asymmetry that had disappeared at rest.
Static compensation is based on resting activity in the vestibular nuclei on the affected side returning over time.
Neurons in these nuclei increase their own excitability, so they start firing again despite the reduced input.
The commissural fibers linking the nuclei on both sides, and the inhibitory influence of the cerebellum, are also readjusted.
So even if the nerve loss is permanent, the activity of the nuclei on both sides comes close to each other again.
A classic observation showing that compensation is a central process is the Bechterew phenomenon.
In animals, if the healthy labyrinth is disabled after the first loss has compensated, a new nystagmus starts in the opposite direction.
This shows that the brain balanced the first loss centrally, and the second loss upsets this new balance.
In some people, for example after vestibular neuritis, the function of the labyrinth or nerve returns partly or fully.
Adaptation is the adjustment of the gain of remaining function; for example, the gain of the vestibulo-ocular reflex, or VOR, increases.
In earlier lessons we also referred to this process as VOR adaptation.
Substitution means replacing missing information with vision, body sense or new eye movement strategies.
For example, the covert saccade, which appears before a head impulse has ended, is a substitution strategy.
Habituation is the gradual decrease of the discomfort response when a movement that triggers symptoms is repeated.
Vestibular rehabilitation exercises are designed to target each of these routes.
In this graph we see head velocity and eye velocity during a fast head movement toward the affected side.
Eye velocity lags behind head velocity; in other words, VOR gain is low and the image slips on the retina.
This retinal slip is an error signal for the cerebellum.
The cerebellum, especially the flocculus, readjusts the gain of the VOR pathway to reduce this error.
For this adjustment to happen, the person needs to move the head while looking at a visual target.
So avoiding head movement slows dynamic compensation.
This schematic graph shows the typical course of symptoms over time after a sudden unilateral loss.
Vertigo at rest and spontaneous nystagmus usually decrease clearly in the first days.
Static symptoms often resolve largely within days to weeks.
Dynamic symptoms brought on by head movement decrease much more slowly and may not always resolve fully.
In fast head movements, VOR gain often does not return fully to normal; substitution strategies close the gap.
Animal studies suggest that the first weeks after the loss are an especially sensitive period for plasticity.
In humans, the exact length of this period is not known; but early, active movement is thought to be helpful.
In the acute phase, the person is advised to start moving safely as soon as nausea and vomiting ease.
A gradual return to daily tasks, rather than staying still in bed for a long time, supports compensation.
It matters that the person makes the movement themselves; being moved passively does not give the same learning.
Lacour and colleagues recommended an active approach that starts early and is tailored to the person.
The rehabilitation program follows the individual plan of the qualified clinician who assessed the person.
Current guidelines state that rehabilitation started early in acute unilateral loss may improve the outcome.
Compensation does not progress at the same speed in everyone; some factors can slow the process.
Long-term use of vestibular suppressant drugs is chief among these factors.
Avoiding head and body movement, or staying in the dark or in bed for long periods, also slows the process.
If sensation from vision or the soles of the feet is weak, as in peripheral neuropathy, the information needed for substitution is reduced.
Cerebellar or brainstem problems affect the very centers that carry out compensation.
Anxiety, depression, migraine and cognitive problems can also affect rehabilitation outcomes negatively.
A fluctuating labyrinth function, as in Meniere's disease, makes it hard for the brain to reach a stable new balance.
By contrast, older age alone does not prevent recovery; older adults also benefit from rehabilitation.

maddeler.metin: Short-term use in the acute phase
Short, low dose may ease participation

cumleler: In the acute phase, a physician may recommend short-term medication for severe nausea and vertigo.
These drugs suppress symptoms; but they may also reduce the signals needed for compensation.
So long-term use of vestibular suppressant drugs has been reported to delay recovery.
The current guideline notes that short-term, low-dose use may make it easier for the person to take part in exercises.
Starting, continuing and stopping medication are the physician's decisions; the clinician consults the referring physician if needed.
The audiologist records the medications used during assessment, because some of them also affect test results.
In a compensated person, symptoms may temporarily return during fatigue, a febrile illness or intense stress.
Alcohol and sedative drugs can also trigger this temporary decline.
A new positional vertigo or a new vestibular event, however, should be assessed separately.
Telling the person about this possibility in advance reduces anxiety when symptoms return.
Putting renewed emphasis on the exercises during these periods often helps return to the earlier level.

sahneler.metin: When monitoring compensation, look at the complaint, not only the test. A person may be functionally well compensated even if the caloric asymmetry persists.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: the asymmetry on caloric testing often stays the same even after compensation.
In other words, a caloric weakness does not show how well the person has compensated.
At follow-up, weigh the complaint, head-shake nystagmus, the saccade pattern on the video head impulse test and balance tests together.
Self-report scales such as the Dizziness Handicap Inventory are also very valuable for tracking functional status.
Static symptoms usually decrease clearly in the first days; dynamic symptoms resolve more slowly and sometimes incompletely.
Static compensation rests on rebalancing resting activity in the vestibular nuclei; the cerebellum guides the process.
Dynamic compensation happens through VOR adaptation, substitution strategies and habituation; all require head movement.
Long-term suppressant use, inactivity, visual and sensory problems, anxiety and migraine can delay the process.

sahneler.soru: What is the most important condition for dynamic compensation?
secenekler: Head movement and a visual target
sahneler.aciklama: VOR adaptation works through _retinal slip_; this needs head movement and a target.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: what is the most important condition for dynamic compensation?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: head movement and a visual target.
Retinal slip during head movement is the error signal the cerebellum needs to readjust VOR gain.
